utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Motoike.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For the record, the Prosecution now calls Dr. Simon Eichner.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Simon Eichner?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Can you please, for us, briefly describe your education background?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I finished my school studies in Munich and then my university studies in Munich in physics and graduated in 1967. Thereafter, I studied at the University of Munich and finished my doctorate there. And in 1981, from 1981 onwards, I worked for the Bavarian criminal police. And later I headed the weapons section of the criminal police and I have remained in this position up to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: So just for clarification, you are currently employed then with the criminal police?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And where is that exactly?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is the criminal police of Bavaria in Munich. It's responsible for Bavaria.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And on 17 March 2006 did you have an opportunity to prepare a report which contained your expert opinion on the possible causal origins for nitrite and/or nitrate deposits on an individual's hands, the scientific conclusions that can be drawn from the findings of nitrate deposits on a person's hands and the use of nitrate or nitrate tests for detecting gunshot residues in the forensic community? Did you prepare a report regarding these issues?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Could we please show the witness 65 ter 364, and actually while that is coming up we have provided -- prepared hard copy binders for the witness today. If we could, with the assistance of the usher, distribute those. And for further clarification because of the number of exhibits, we actually have these broken into two binders. There's a separate soft cover binder that contains the copies of the reports that I expect to tender with this witness. And we could display 65 ter 364, please. And the hard copy of this particular report is provided in the separate soft cover binder at tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And, Dr. Eichner, you have the hard copy of the report in front much you but also on the computer screen there is displayed a copy of the same report. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Is this the report that you prepared on 17 March 2006?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is the report which I prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Does this report also have two attachments to it as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Actually, Doctor, can I show you on the screen. If we could please show 65 ter 365, which is tab 3 of today's hardcover binder.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the annex, the annexes. They are here present in the file. And this is the way I submitted the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And I believe the first annex, as you termed it, is being displayed on the screen presently. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And the hard copy shows that it is an excerpt from a publication by a professor doctor out of the university of Bonn. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And if we could please also show 65 ter 366, which is tab 4 of today's hardcover binder. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And, Doctor, this is now being displayed on the screen. Do you recognise this as being the second attachment and/or annex to this report dated 17 March 2006?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is the first page of the second annex.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And this particular article is entitled "Summary of the FBI Laboratory's Gunshot Residue (GSR) Symposium" and it is dated May 31 through June 3, 2005. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. That was a summary made during that symposium.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And are both of these two articles, the two attachments that we've just seen, are these referenced and relied upon in the report dated 17 March 2006?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The reference is made to the two articles in a paragraph about the presence of nitrate and the importance of nitrate in the -- in scientific circles in the international community.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would ask to tender the report which is 65 ter 364 as well as the two attachments located at 65 ter 365 and 65 ter 366.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 364 will become exhibit P421. 65 ter 365 will become Exhibit P422. And 65 ter 366 will become Exhibit P423, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Dr. Eichner, as part of your occupation and training, do you keep abreast of the scientific literature and studies related to the various detection methods of gunshot residue?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I keep myself abreast of scientific literature. And there is an international exchange of experience under way in which we participate, and we also have a national exchange of experience and I'm one of the figures in this exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And as part of that exchange and the education that you partake in, are you familiar with the paraffin glove test?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I know this test from the literature, but we, for our part, do not use this test, and I can explain the reasons why, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: We can get to that in just a second. Could I first ask you, what does this test, this paraffin glove test indicate the presence of?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The test described here in the annex of my report, and there was -- referred to a report of the Macedonian police and it is to test the presence of nitrate through dephenylamine and the reagents is able to prove the presence of nitrate by turning it into a certain colour. There's a chemical reaction and through the reaction one can determine whether certain substances are present, among which nitrates in -- by means of reagent.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And you indicated that you yourself do not use this paraffin glove test. Based on your training and experience, do forensic scientists usually work with this kind of test to detect gunshot particles?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: No. In Germany, I don't think anyone uses it. And as far as I know internationally, there does not seem to be any use of it, because there could be positive reactions which are not based on the presence of nitrate through this test. There could be other substances which have nitrate in them but are not gunpowder residue, so it's not specific enough to determine gunshot residue itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. And, Doctor, keeping this paraffin glove test in mind, I'd like to actually focus you now on specific topics or a couple of tops relating to the test that you have discussed in your report that's dated 17 March 2006. In pages 8 through 14 you discuss the scientific conclusions, if any, that can be drawn from the paraffin glove tests that were performed on 15 individuals from Ljuboten village. These tests were performed by the Macedonian forensic technicians in August of 2001. And also, on pages 1 and 2 of your report, you indicate the documents from the Macedonian authorities which relate to these paraffin glove tests that you reviewed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Drawing your attention to the documents relating to the results of these 15 individuals that you reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And for the Chamber's and the witness's convenience and all parties, these have actually been provided in the hard binders at tabs 9 through 23; however, since these are already admitted exhibits actually under exhibit number P00050, and because they are already delineated in Dr. Eichner's report, in order to save time I will not go through each of these with the doctor at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: But, doctor, you reviewed what was described by the Macedonian authorities in each document as the results of the paraffin glove tests for 15 individuals. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I got out of the documents that I received.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you please tell us whether it is discernible from the documents that you reviewed as to how the tests, these paraffin glove tests were performed as to each of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: As far as I know from the documents, imprints were made with wax and I would imagine that this means that the hands were covered with wax or a waxy substance, were moistened with such a substance and then the glove created by the wax was taken off and the inner part was sprayed with diphenylamine to cause certain chemical reactions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And in your opinion after reviewing the results of these tests what scientific conclusions, if any, could you draw?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: There's two different cases here. Nitrates are not only to be found in gunpowder. They are also components of other substances in daily life - Dr. Stein will speak about this later, about the substances which contain nitrate, substances found in day-to-day life. I can only mention things like fertilisers or food or pickled meats and cured meats and different foods. But I think Dr. Stein will talk about this in greater detail. Nitrates are found not only in gunpowder but they're also found in other substances in day-to-life. Let us assume for a moment that the proof of the presence of carried out by the Macedonian police say that particles were present through the diphenylamine test. If we assume that the particle did not come from gunpowder, then it could equally cause a positive reaction. Dr. Stein will discuss this in detail because he has carried out experiments and I have seen some of his experiences to see which substances of day-to-day life do cause a positive reaction. On the other hand, if we assume that the particles which cause a reaction do stem from gunpowder, if we assume that this is proven, then we would see that the hands are covered with substances deriving from gunpowder and what could be proven by that. Normally you would see particles on a hand which has shot an arm, a gun. You would see burnt or partially burnt particles of gunpowder, more or less burnt, with a very high level of nitrate, and the particles would remain on the hand of the person who used the rifle or the gun. So, a positive reaction would correspond to the hand which has used a weapon. However, our experience over the last 25 years has shown that there are a lot of other explanations for residue, for gunpowder -- or for residue to be on the hands of people without them having used a weapon. These other possibilities can occur when someone has had contact with another hand which has used a weapon. If you give -- if you shake someone's hand who has used a weapon, then you will get nitrate particles on your hand, and this could be another possible explanation. Or it could happen that someone, with his hand, defends himself against a weapon being directed at him and the -- a cloud of residue would be in the air and it would get onto the hand of the person defending himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Doctor --

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: So you would see the particles on the hand in this case too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Could I stop you there for a second. Could I actually focus you a little bit on with respect to the findings that you made after your review of the results, if I could just direct your attention to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: If we could display also on e-court. It's P 00050, 65 ter 15.11. In e-court it's pages 30 through 31 for the English and 106 through 107 for the Macedonian. It is located at tab 9 of today's hardcover binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Dr. Eichner, do you see the document that is being displayed in front of you? The hard copy is also located at tab 9 of the binder. And if I could just direct your attention to the top of the document. It says Republic of Macedonia, Ministry of Interior, criminological techniques department. It is dated 14 August 2001, Skopje. And its subject is analysis of traces of fire-arms and it goes on to speak of findings with respect to a person by the name Ali Riza, which is referred to the first paragraph. And it indicates that an analysis of the submitted foils has been conducted. The reaction used was positive for the right hand foil, i.e., presence of nitrate particles on the hand was determined. Do you see that, doctor?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And is this one of the results that you referred to and you reviewed actually in your report?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Yes, I did have this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And if we could please display, I believe the third -- second page in English and the second page in Macedonian of this particular document. And on the left of the screen, Doctor, there's what appears to be sketches of two hands. And there's an asterisk actually noted that is visible in the right hand on the right side of the page. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And was this also a part of this particular test result that you reviewed in formulating your opinions with respect to your report?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I did have the document with this number, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. If we could show one more, please. It's P 00050 as well, 65 ter 15.12 located at tab 10 of today's hardcover binders. In English in e-court it is pages 32 through 33; in Macedonian, it's pages 108 to 109. And, Doctor, similarly with this document that's now being displayed, again it is from the Republic of Macedonia, Ministry of Interior, criminalistic police, dated 14 August 2001. And do you see again it says, subject, analysis of traces of nitrate particles. This report indicates a name of K-j-a-m-u-r-a-n Rexhepi, and it indicates that an analysis of the submitted foils has been conducted. The reaction used was positive for the foil of the right hand of the aforementioned person; that is, presence of nitrate particles on the hand was determined. Do you see that, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And attached to that, if we could show page 2 in the Macedonian, please, which is also page 2 of the English. And again, Doctor, like the other document we just showed, there is a sketch of two hands, and on this sketch they're indicated handwritten asterisks on the right hand. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And again, is this a document that you also reviewed as part of your report?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I had this document too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And is it your understanding that the asterisks indicated on these sketches that were provided to you indicate the -- where there was a positive reaction for nitrate or nitrite?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is how I understood it from the text of the written part of the -- the report speaks of nitrate particles, so I assume it is a question of these particles here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And out of the 15 -- let me ask you this first: You reviewed 15 documents that looked like this, that is, the first page indicated the presence of nitrate/nitrite particles and then there was attached hand -- sketches of the hands with asterisks indicated on them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Let me count them for a moment. There are 15 documents that I had here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And I guess my question was, were they similar to these, that is, that they had a cover page that indicated there was a positive presence detected and then a sketch of the hands with the asterisks indicated on them?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes. The texts were more or less the same in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. And in your review of these 15 results for these individuals, can I ask you what's the most number of asterisks that you had seen on the hands of these individuals, as a -- from these results?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The greatest number of asterisks was 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. And is that significant somehow in the scientific community as far as a result for determining the presence of gunpowder residue?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: No, I would not say so. Such a result does not lead to any particular interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. Could I also show you an additional sketch that did you not have as part of your report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Could we please display for the doctor 65 ter 995; it also bears ERN N0063580-N0063580 and it is located at tab 24 of today's hard binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And, Dr. Eichner, actually could I just follow up on something that you indicated earlier. You had said that the number of particle-- of asterisks, being at 3 at the most, on these 15 persons was not -- could not lead to any particular interpretation. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The three asterisks which show the presence of nitrate particles, if they are that, could have got on to the hand by various means. There are several possible explanations for such the small amount of particles on the hands. It could be the firing of a weapon by the hand in question, but it could also be other contacts and circumstances. There are many possibilities, and as such, there is no definite explanation as to how the particles got on to the hand. So there is nothing very specific one can say about the origin of the presence of the particles.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And, Doctor, assuming that these asterisks did indicate the presence of nitrate or nitrite particles that came from gunshot residue, what other things or factors would you look at to actually make a conclusion, if you can, that these were gunshot particles coming from a person who had actually fired a handgun or a weapon?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The first step would be to prove whether the particles here were actually gun residue, gunpowder residue or whether they could derive from other sources. This could be done analytically. There are chemical processes to do this, chemical tests and there are apparatus. For instance, there is the scanning electronic microscope to see whether we are dealing here with gunpowder or not. If this is proven positively in tests, one could then try to limit the origins of the presence of the particles. One possibility would be to look at the surface distribution of the particles to see if there are any limitations or patterns, and this is what we -- this is how we would proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And based on your review of the 15 results, could you make any determinations on -- based on a surface distribution of the particles?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: No, in none of the cases could I do this, because the surface distribution was not specific enough to allow any explanation of how the residues got on to the hands. In none of the cases was there an obvious result or were we able to limit the explanation to find a specific explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. If we could then look at this additional sketch which was not incorporated in your report. It is displayed on the screen now, Doctor, and on the left side there are apparently the front -- the back and the palm side -- the back side and the palm side of both the right and the left human hands and there are some asterisks also indicated on this particular diagram. And just for your knowledge, Doctor, we have in this court already received testimony from a forensic medical doctor with respect to him conducting a paraffin glove test on a person by the name of Atulla Qaili. And this is on pages 2292 through 2293 of the Court transcript. And the Dr. Jakovski testified as to a particular document that indicated the presence of nitrate/nitrite particles based on the paraffin glove test performed on this particular individual.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And for the record, that exhibit was P 00049, which is also 65 ter 13.9. And, Doctor, looking at this particular sketch and the asterisks that are noted, and again assuming that these asterisks note the presence or positive reaction for nitrite/nitrate particles on the hands, in your opinion, what scientific conclusions can be drawn from this particular sketch?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Here again, my evaluation is no different from that for the other sketches we've seen. This distribution of particles here, there are a few more particles here, but they are nonetheless too few to explain the surface distribution. They could stem from the firing of a weapon or from many other origins.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Are there a sufficient -- I know that we discussed at most, three particles being present in the other reports, not giving you a surface area distribution or a sense of the surface area distribution. Looking at this particular sketch are you able to make a determination, though, is there a sufficient number of particles indicated for an assessment of the surface area distribution, if you understand me?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: With this distribution here, I would call this a discrete distribution of particles, which means it is not possible to derive conclusions from such a distribution. If we only have three particles as we did on the other sketches, it is simply not sufficient to draw a conclusion or to come to a more specific conclusion about the origin of the particles.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And, Doctor, you spoke earlier, right before I cut you off - and I apologise for that - of the possibility of contamination in your report. Can contamination occur with respect to tests like the paraffin glove test?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: If one assumes that during the conducting of the test one -- that the test -- if one assumes that the tests are carried out carefully in a laboratory, then contamination would be unlikely. But it depends how the tests are carried out. In such a case I don't really see that much contamination could have occurred during the testing here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Well, in -- let's just take it outside of this particular test that is displayed on the screen. In your opinion, can the lack of preservation of the hands of a person who is eventually tested for nitrate/nitrite particles, could that lead to contamination?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that could bring about a contamination. If we take into consideration what sort of influences hands are submitted to, the -- from the original presence of the particles until the test, I can assure you there are a whole range of possibilities of contamination. For instance, we have seen in our lab tests that people who have been arrested and have had shackles put on their hands have received particles from the person arresting them, because most police vehicles-- most police vehicles, for instance, transport weapons on the back seat of their vehicles. And if the persons arrested sit on the benches where the weapons were, they will be contaminated, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Can I ask you also whether, speaking about this transfer aspect, can I ask you whether or not you think it is possible that contamination can occur if someone's hands that were eventually tested for nitrite/nitrate particles were hit on by weapons that had recently been fired?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is indeed possible. That is a possible source of contamination. It is very likely that when touching a weapon with gunpowder residue on it that you would thus transfer that residue to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Could I show you two documents which you also referenced in your report. These are the opinions of the ministry -- actually from the Ministry of Interior, forensic sector, in relation to the paraffin glove tests that you received.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Could we please show P 00050. It was previously known as 65 ter 15.7. That is 25 of today's hardcover binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And, Doctor, the English version on the left of the screen, if I could just run through it with you. It says Republic of Macedonia, Ministry of the Interior, criminalistic police, criminalistic technique department. It's dated 27 August 2001. It's addressed to Basic Court Skopje II. And it mentions the names of particular individuals and then it also speaks of the detection of traces of gunpowder particles in the third paragraph. And then it goes on to state: "Seeing as there is a limited number of sources in everyday life of a person where contamination with nitrate particles can occur, their presence of the hands of a person is an indication that that person has fired a fire-arm." The next paragraph reads: "Based on their form, location and positioning, it can be determined with a great probability that these nitrate particles originate from gunpowder." And, Doctor, if I could just ask you: Is this one of the reports that had for review?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I did have such a document with that number for review.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And if can we could please show an additional document. It's P 00050, it's tab 26 of today's binders. Was previously 65 ter 15.8.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And, Doctor, this particular document reads the same in the left-hand corner. The date is 28 August 2001. Again, it's addressed to Basic Court Skopje II. The subject is additional opinion. And this document, like the other one, goes on to mention names of persons that were tested, and then in the fourth paragraph down it says: "Seeing as there is a limited number of sources in everyday life of a person where contamination with nitrate particles can occur, their presence on the hands of a person is an indication that that person has fired a fire-arm. Based on their form, location and positioning, it can be determined with a great probability that these nitrate particles originate from gunpowder." Do you see that, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And is this also another report that you had for review in formulating your report?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, such -- such a document with that number was also reviewed by me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And bearing in mind the last two paragraphs of each of these documents that I just showed you - they read somewhat similarly - can you tell us based on your training and experience, do you have an opinion as to the finding made in these particular paragraphs in these two documents?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Referring to paragraph 4, I can say that the statement about the presence of nitrate particles being an indication that a person fired a fire-arm is not wrong. But the statement is not complete, because it doesn't take into consideration that there is a number of possibilities for particles to come to a person's hand, I mean gunshot residue particles, without that person ever having fired a fire-arm. So it is not a false statement but it isn't a complete one either. About the last paragraph, which I'm reading here, based on their form, location, positioning, et cetera, about this I can say that this does not correspond to our experience; namely, that using a visual method and a method for proving the presence of nitrate that this -- these methods are suitable for proving gunshot residue. Of course it cannot be ruled out that these particles might be gunshot residue, but if you want to be more certain, you would have to apply analytical procedures of -- from chemistry or physics.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. And would some of those procedures be the testing that you also indicated as additional testing that could be done, that is the electron microscope, I believe you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The Raster electron microscope is the usual tool of proving the presence of particles of one micrometre, the size of one micrometre. That is the method upon which most international experts rely. When -- and I cannot see anyone or, rather, I don't know anyone who would rely on such a method to prove the presence of gunshot residue. It would be best to use chemical procedures such as a liquid chromotography, so would you dissolve the particles in a liquid and then analyse the ingredients of that liquid. Dr. Stein will be able to say more about that because that method can be used to directly prove the substances present and the liquid analysed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: If I could just clarify one part of your last answer, doctor. You said: "I don't know anybody who would rely on such a method to prove the presence of gunshot residue." What method are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the method of exclusively relying on the presence of nitrate particles without conducting additional analyses to prove whether gunshot residue was present. I don't know any expert who would -- who would proceed in such a way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. Doctor, if I can draw your attention now to 15 January 2007, did you prepare an additional report regarding your expert opinion on three particular weapons that were received from the Macedonian Ministry of Interior which were handed over to you by the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Three weapons were sent to me, and I wrote an expert opinion about those dated 15th of January, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Could we please display 65 ter 1040. It is located at tab 27 of today's soft binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Doctor, the report I believe you're referencing is displayed on the screen here. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And is this the report that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is the first page of the report that I wrote, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And did this particular report contain your opinion as to comparisons that you made between these three weapons that were handed over to you and weapons which were depicted in a video that was also provided to you by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Correct. The exhibits were accompanied by a CD containing a video-clip and in that video-clip for a few seconds three weapons could be seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: If I could just turn your attention to your report for a second. It appears to have three attachments to this report that contain photographs of the three weapons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is correct. This report, too, did have -- did have enclosures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please tender this particular report with its attachments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P424, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Doctor, you mention a video that was provided to you as well. If I could please show a video-clip to the doctor. Which is P00041.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. The Time of the clip is 06 minutes, 8 seconds to 06 minutes, 21 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Doctor, if I can draw your attention to the screen on your right. There will be a video-clip paying in a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Doctor, have you seen that this last clip showed three weapons. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And does this video-clip look similar to the one that you reviewed and utilized in making your comparisons to formulate your opinions in the report dated 15 January 2007?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this video-clip clearly as shown to me now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And, Doctor, there were three weapons depicted in that video-clip. What kind of identification did you assign to the weapons depicted in the video-clip for purposes of your evaluation?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: We tried to -- to extract still images from that video-clip. We used [indiscernible] that is usually used for such purposes, and these still images then were compared to the picture that I had of the weapons, and then I tried to find similarities. At first I tried to establish whether the weapons were of the same type, and they were. In this case we're speaking about two weapons belonging to the Kalashnikov family of weapons and a submachine-gun belonging to the Thompson family of weapons. So this was -- this was indeed the case. The investigation was continued to -- to focus on the individual characteristics of these weapons, how much detail could be seen, and after this second stage, we focussed on individual characteristics, and thus we arrived at our results.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And in your report you reference an upper weapon, a middle weapon and a lower weapon. Is that referencing the weapons as they are displayed in the video-clip that we just saw?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. According to my memory, the video-clip first shows a weapon that is in the upper part of the image. Then it -- the camera is moved to the lower weapon, and in the centre there is a Thompson submachine-gun, the barrel of which is more or less parallel to the other two. There was also a weapon, the barrel of which is pointing to the left but it cannot be seen in the -- in the video-clip in full. You can only see the front part, but as far as I remember, the butt cannot be seen in the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. If we can start with what you termed to be the lower weapon, and you said that you had conducted analysis, a comparison between the actual weapons that were provided to you and the lower weapon in the video-clip. Could you tell us what findings, if any, you were able to make when you compared this lower weapon with one of the -- with the three weapons that you received?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: It can be seen that in the front part of this lower weapon the-- the front part of the stock, there -- you can see some things that is -- that are not usually seen in Kalashnikov rifles manufactured in the large series. What I noticed is the fact that this lower part of the front stock is fastened by pins. This is not usual. Then the barrel is -- is manufactured in such a way that it has in steps. That is not usual for Kalashnikov-type weapons. And there are also conic transitions. This is it also not typical of Kalashnikov weapons in their original version. These characteristics were -- could be observed in the weapon that I was given to analyse, especially these steps in the barrel and the pins used to fasten the front stock. It is unknown in other Kalashnikov-type weapons. And this is a strong indication that the weapon I received for examination, and I designated as exhibit 001, from this I draw the conclusion that these two weapons could be identical, but the image -- the image quality is too poor so I cannot say for sure that this -- it is the self-same weapon but there is a strong indication of their identity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And with respect to the upper weapon, what findings, if any, were you able to make with respect to that weapon and the actual weapons provided to you?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: What is conspicuous in the upper weapon is that it has no butt. And furthermore, the upper part of the front end of the stock has a dark line. Also, the rear part on the right side, we can see in the video that there is a spot which is irregular. In the particular weapon provided to me, I observed a clear damaged spot, and it seems to be the imprint of a massive pair of tongs such as used by plumbers. And so this is -- seems like the -- so this is an indication that these weapons are -- could be the ones shown in the video. But here too I must say due to the poor quality of the video I cannot be positive about that. There are indications, however, that we cannot rule out that this weapon, the weapon shown in the video is the one that I examined.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And as far as the middle weapon, did you make any findings with respect to that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Talking about the middle weapon, I noticed some things, especially on the left part of the -- of the butt. Therefore, conspicuous artifacts that can be seen in the video and they can also be found on the butt or shaft of the weapon provided to me and -- at the same place. On the receiver, on the -- above the -- above gliding parts of the receiver, there is a similar series of lighter and darker lines as seen in the video. It is possible that these are spots with a different reflexiveness that could be the result of corrosive processes. Corrosive processes are highly individual, highly particular, and it is extremely unlikely that corrosion will be exactly the same in two objects. So if these are -- so if these traces are indeed traces of corrosion, then the patterns that will be created would be highly individualised. If we look at the spot on the weapon provided to me, we will see a pattern of lighter and darker lines which corresponds to what can be seen in the video-clip to that effect. So if that pattern was created by corrosion, the pattern that can be seen in the video, then it strongly corresponds to the pattern on the weapon provided to me. If I try to evaluate all these indications, I would say that it is highly likely that the weapon in the video-clip is the very weapon submitted to me. However, there is a certain likelihood that there might be another weapon with -- with such a pattern. I cannot be positive due to the poor quality of the video, but the likelihood is small.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Doctor, were you also asked to examine bullets, bullet cores and bullet fragments that were reported to you to have been found near the bodies of certain deceased persons in Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is correct. That was a third request for me to examine bullets and fragments.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And did you prepare a report dated 16 April 2007 with respect to your findings?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes. My opinion is dated 16th of April, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Could we please show 65 ter number 1041 which is tab 31 of today's soft cover binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And, Doctor, is this report that is displayed on the screen, is that the report that you speak of?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, this is the letter accompanying the opinion that I sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Okay. And beyond that letter, do you see the actual report in the hard copy before you?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The letter -- or, rather, a report was attached to that letter. However, I cannot see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Could we please display page 2 of this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Dr. Eichner, is the cover page of your report now being displayed on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now. This is the report that I wrote and it is dated 16th of April, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P425, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And, Dr. Eichner, in relation to this particular report, the identification numbers, if we could scroll down a little bit on the English version as well as the Macedonian, please. Actually, it would be page 3 of the Macedonian -- I mean, 2, sorry. Doctor, the report indicates package ERF number and then there is a designation of BA-28, BA-29 on the report. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And these identification numbers that you utilised in your report, were these identification numbers the ones that were provided to you at the time when you received these particular objects from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I received the ammunition fragments in plastic bags and these were the designations on the bags. The individual bullets were packed in -- in their individual bags and I designated the -- these ERF numbers to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Your Honours, to assist the Chamber, the identification numbers, understanding Dr. Eichner' report, the identification numbers assigned to each ammunition fragment or ammunition is the ICTY reference number assigned by then Office of the Prosecutor investigator Howard Tucker, who will testify pursuant to Rule 92 bis about these particular fragments and pieces of evidence and the chain of custody for such.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Dr. Eichner, as part of this particular examination did you conduct comparisons between the bullets -- bullet cores and bullet fragments with the three weapons that you had already received and referenced in your report dated 15 January 2007?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I compared the ammunition fragments provided to me to those individual parts of ammunition, and we obtained pieces of ammunition from the three particular weapons and those pieces of ammunitions carried the individual properties of those weapons, upon which we tried to establish whether the ammunition fragments designated with ERF and BA numbers, whether these had the same sorts of marks from which conclusions could be drawn whether or not these fragments were actually fired from any one of these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: And were you able to make any conclusive findings with respect to these evaluations that you conducted?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: We were able to draw conclusions from the evaluation, and these conclusions are shown in my report on page 7 in the table, and we came to the conclusion that the Thompson submachine-gun couldn't have been the one from which those fragments were fired because that weapon has a different calibre. This submachine-gun was of calibre .45 ACP and it is impossible to shoot 7.62-millimetre calibre ammunition from it. Neither was it possible to fire 7.92-millimetre ammunition from that submachine-gun. Talking about the Kalashnikov-type rifles, it would have been possible due to the identity of calibre that these ammunition fragments were shot from one of them except for the 7.92-metre bullet because it differs in calibre. As for the fragments of 7.62-millimetre calibre, what can be said is that these weapons cannot be ruled out as the ones from which some of the ammunition was fired, but we cannot be positive for any individual case that they were the ones from which they were fired. Likewise, we can be sure that in certain cases some fragments could not have been fired from these weapons, because we found some class characteristics in these ammunitions that make that impossible. But due to the quality of the ammunition fragments received, we cannot draw a certain conclusion that any one of these weapons was used to actually fire the ammunitions received.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The questions arises - I'm not sure whether I'm looking at Mr. Mettraux or Ms. Residovic; I see Mr. Mettraux - whether it would be practical to spend the next seven or eight minutes or whether we should have a break now and resume and commence. What would you suggest, Mr. Mettraux?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll ask for a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will do that then and have the first break now. We will resume at ten minutes past 4.00 for Mr. Mettraux's cross-examination of Dr. Eichner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, doctor. My name is Guenal Mettraux and together with Ms. Edina Residovic, I'm representing Mr. Boskoski. Doctor, we've received your reports and we've had time to consult those carefully, so I just would like to put a number of propositions to you with a view to limit the scope of our discussion. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very well. Is that correct, sir, that your evidence is that the paraffin glove is a rather unreliable test to detect gunpowder residue and that, in fact, it is reliable only insofar as it detects nitrite particles. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Not even that. If you use the paraffin test with diphenylamine, then there are other substances which could cause a positive reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes. And you've indicated also that the nitrite particles that could be detected by the diphenylamine chemical reaction into not only gunpowder but also other substances including I think you've indicated some kinds of pickled food. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible. Nitrates are found in substances which are not related to gunshot residues.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct, also, Doctor, that the chemical reaction with diphenylamine is used generally in combination with a visual analysis or visual identification of the particles that have been identified chemically. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That's what I understood from the reports from Macedonia, that they carried out not only the chemical analysis but also a visual analysis, whatever they understand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that visual analysis could be done, for instance, with an optical microscope. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But I do not know how the investigation was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you will agree if that were indeed the method that had been used, that is, an optical microscope their quality, so to say, of the conclusion or analysis that would be drawn would be only as good as the expert who's carried out this analysis. Is that correct? In other words, it is dependant on the expertise or experience of the person carrying out the test.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: In all such analyses experience is one of the main factors to maintain quality and give results.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do I also understand your evidence properly that you are not suggesting that the results of the tests carried out by the Macedonian authorities or the conclusion which they draw are wrong; what is your evidence is, sir, is that you take issue with the reliability of these results because of the method used. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The results of the method or the results in the report are that gunpowder particles are present and this is correct to that extent, that one is drawing a conclusion from a very small indication that it could be that. It is a -- if it is a positive result, the result is very much borderline.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you yourself, Doctor, are not suggesting either way; you are not saying it was or it wasn't gunpowder residue. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: It could be said that way, that a positive result from a diphenylamine test does not necessarily prove the presence of gunpowder, of gunpowder residue.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir, that you would not be in a position yourself to make any conclusion as to the exact nature of the particles because you did not have access to either the gloves or the particles themselves. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That's not quite what I would say. The fact that I don't think you could draw conclusions here does not stem from the type of test but, rather, from the fact that if the particles were gunpowder particles, then one could not draw any conclusions as to how these particles got on to the hands. That has got nothing to do with the diphenylamine test.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I apologise, doctor. I think my question was not very precise and I will have comment on the issue that you just raise. But my question was about your particular ability in this particular case to determine whether or not the particles in question originated from gunpowder. And my question, Doctor, was: Is that correct that you were not in a position to make your own conclusion in this respect, because you had no access to either the gloves or the particles themselves. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is not true. The conclusion that no definitive decision can be made about the origins of the particles does not depend on the type of particles, whether they are nitrate particles or not. That is quite a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But would it be correct that the availability of the particles would be one factor for you, in addition to others, to be able to make a definite -- definitive judgement in relation to this matter. Would that be correct? You would need the particles, in other words.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: No. No, that's not true. The presence of the particles here, which contained nitrate, well, the conclusion was drawn here that it was probably gunpowder. This is one possible answer to the issue. Another problem involved here is whether these particles found here derive from the shooting of a weapon from a hand. This is quite a different issue from the first, and this first issue, trying to determine the origin of the particles, whether it is from a gun-shooting hand, is not possible here because the particles were perhaps not sufficiently analysed and it is not possible to draw such a conclusion because the origin of the particles could be from a weapon or could be from some other mechanism. They are two completely different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes. And staying perhaps with the first of these two question, Doctor, the question of the nature of the particle, is that correct that you are not able to say more than it could have been gunpowder and it could have been something else. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Because of the methods used, one could assume that it is not -- cannot be excluded that it is gunpowder residue. But one cannot say anything more than that. This is not proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I'll come back to this in a minute, sir, but the second question or the second part of the test which you underline, namely the origin or the source of the residue in question, you made the point that the manner in which the particles could have come on the hands of this particular individual could have come from shooting a gun or from otherwise using a gun or from other modes of contamination. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in your report you've raised a number of, I should say scientific hypotheses as to how the particles could have come on the hand other than by the shooting of the gun. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But I would like to add that these are empirical date not scientific data, empirical data gathered over the last few years.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the precision, doctor, because that was my next question. You are not suggesting in your report, are you, that this particular hypothesis would apply to any of the particular 16 tests that were carried out. You are simply assuming that scientifically or empirically, as you pointed out, they are possible explanations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: There is -- we know of experience that certain distribution on a firing hand could also be produced by other means, other than the shooting of a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And just to come back to my question, Doctor, you were not in any way suggesting that any of the six or so hypotheses which you laid down in your report would apply to any of the particular 15 tests that were provided to you when you prepared your report. Is that correct? You did not in any way suggest that one could be matched with the other. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I don't know quite how I should say it. The conclusion from the distribution of the particles, the conclusion that could be drawn and was drawn by the Macedonian police, in my view, there is no positive proof of how the -- of the origin of the particles, of how they got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And my question following on this one would be that it's also true of the other hypotheses which you put forward; you are not claiming that any of those would be the correct explanation in relation to any of the 15 tests that were given to you. Those are simply empirical hypotheses. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: You speak constantly about hypotheses. These are empirical experience. They're not hypotheses. Because of the distribution of the particles we see that there are several possibilities to explain the origin of the particles. And more cannot be said.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps before we proceed, if the second microphone of Dr. Eichner could be switched on? There's another matter simply for the record, Your Honour. We have counted 16 tests, 16 persons have been tested for the paraffin, and as my colleague pointed out there are only 15 results available but there have been 16 tests, according to other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Doctor, these empirical experiences, as you call them, have been conducted in -- not in the context of this particular case but in the context of other laboratory tests or in the context of other cases. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. This is experience from real cases over the last 20 or 25 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, Doctor, before we turn to these various hypotheses, I would like to ask you that, is it correct that in addition to the chemical reaction, whether you are using diphenylamine or other chemical products, can be -- the probability is, let's say, that the particular particles in questions are ones of gunpowder origin can be narrowed down and they can be narrowed down by all sort of techniques or mechanism. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: There are technical means nowadays for hands covered with certain types of particles, to draw probabilities about the origins, about their origins as to whether they are gunpowder or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct also that some of those methods are more reliable than others. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: It depends on the methods. Tell me the methods you are referring to and I can give you my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: For example, you have indicated the electron scanning method. That would be considered a reliable method. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The scanning electron microscope is used to investigate all sorts of particles, not only nitrate particles, all sorts of particles to analyse them. That is different from a pure nitrate analysis and is much better than the other test.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you've indicated it doesn't only test the nitrate, it also tests the primary particles. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The test is not carried out for nitrate on the SEM. The SEM analyses particles as to their contents. We have seen from many gunpowder residue particles that most of the cartridges have specific elements which can be seen under a microscope and the main element in the residue are lead, barium and antimon and there is a certain form to the particles which is typical of residue, gunpowder residue, and this comes from a liquification after a high temperature, a melting of the particles, and there is a large possibility, probability here in such a case that the particles are gunpowder residue if one carries out such an analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Am I correct to understand from your words, from the use of the words large possibility and probability that even such a technique would not give you absolute certainty as to the nature and origin of the particles in question. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That would be correct to the extent that not all particles from gunpowder residue have a high significancy. One has to look for particles which have a high level of significancy and such as would be the case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So the answer to the question would be that it would not give you an absolute certainty as to the nature of the particle, is that correct, is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: There is no absolute certainty in science.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, do you know of a test called atomic absorption? Is that a test or a technique you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes. The atomic absorption spectroscopy is another method which is used.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is, it in your view, a reliable mechanism to distinguish between different types of particles and whether in particular those particle could be of gunpowder origin?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Atomic absorption microscopy has one disadvantage. It can only prove the presence of certain elements. It does not make any conclusion about the form of the particles so -- and the method is very sensitive, but the disadvantage is that the form and shape of the particles is not analysed or investigated at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that, Doctor, that was the next set of question. You will agree that indeed the shape or the form of a particular particle is relevant to determining the nature or the possible nature, in any case, of that particle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The form of a particle is one thing, but in itself it's only half of what we need. The contents of the particles are also significant. Particles, these particles which have liquified, which has melted can be a result of many chemical processes, so there are two elements. One is the form of the particle, and the other -- and the elements in the -- the contents of the particle.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Doctor. And is that correct that the form of the particle could be established even with a rather less sophisticated mechanism such as an optical microscope. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: It depends on the size of the particle. If we are only dealing with the external form of the particle up to, say, 10 millimetres, then a microscope -- 0.1 millimetres, then a microscope would suffice, but one to ten micrometres, if that is being analysed, then I don't know such a microscope would suffice for analysis. So you do need the right apparatus for the right test.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And should the particle in question be large enough to be identifiable with the microscope, Doctor, it would also be able for the expert to determine whether the particle was burnt in whole or in part. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: It is possible with a microscope or at least indications could be -- could be gained. If we see the partially burned forms of the particles, we could see that the particles have been carbonised in part, charred, part of it has been turned into carbon dioxide. You can see that on the surface of the particle, it's a bit darker. The particle looks irregular or burnt in an irregular manner, at least on its surface one can see that. And this can serve as an indication, for instance, that it was a propellant residue because here we also have plastic residue. It wouldn't be simply a propellant.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, just taking the propellant for a minute, Doctor, if you were to identify propellants that wasn't burned with a microscope, would you then be able to compare such propellant with propellant from ammunition which you would have in your possession, let's say to compare whether the two would match. Is that technically feasible?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: One can always compare things. And if one sees common features, one has an indication that it is -- that it could be the same substance. However, if you know that other substances could have the same external form, other types of particles, then you have to continue, go even further with your analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So comparing the two could at least limit the range of possible explanation for the nature of the particles in question. Is that a fair proposition?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question. Could you perhaps repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Certainly. If -- if the scientist or the expert who would be extracting unburned particles of propellant, would he then be able or she then be able to compare those particles with let's say particles taken from a cartridge or a bullet that hasn't been used with a view to determining whether they could have come from the same source, whether one could be, if you want, from the same origin than the unburned propellant particle?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Usually the form of partially burnt particles has changed compared to the original form, so direct comparison would not bring about any particular results. We do know from experience that indicators could be one that -- or there would be an indication that if the particles are investigated, we could find out under a microscope that it could be such a partially burnt particle. But there are other plastic particles which burn in the same manner, so, as I have said, if you want to be really sure, you have to carry out further analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'd like to go back for a second to your evidence of a moment ago where you pointed out there were essentially two factors of importance in such analysis - and correct me if I'm wrong in paraphrasing, but you said it was the shape of the particle in question and the content of that particular particle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I'll stay for a second with the question of the shape of that particular particle. Is that correct that the determination that would be made of the shape of the particle in question would allow the expert whatever the means used to exclude possible source of nitrate as explanation for the nitrate in question? Is that a fair proposition?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. We're talking about two completely different things here. The classes of particles that are -- that are analysed under the -- with the microscope or with a scan microscope are particles which have melted completely and have a size of 1 to 50 micrometres; whereas the particles you're referring to are particles of a 10th of a millimetre size that have not been turned into ash as part of the residue, and here, if we analyse the form, we can see that we cannot exclude an origin as a propellant -- propellant as an origin. You have to analyse the contents of the particles to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sorry. My question, Doctor, perhaps it was not so good. If you were to identify a particular particle and you would be able to look at the shape of that particle in question through a microscope or otherwise, is it correct that this visual inspection of the particle would allow you to say, for instance, this is not a particle coming from salami, for example, which is a sort of nitrate. Is it fair to say that the shape of the particle would allow the expert to at least set aside a number of possible source of nitrate? And I'm not talking specifically about the gunpowder here.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: If we stick to this comparison between gunshot residue and salami, it would probably be possible to make a distinction unless the salami had previously been destroyed by a very strong thermal processing, in that case, yes, you would be right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, Doctor, perhaps leaving the salami aside for a minute, would you agree that an expert would have conducted that sort of test dozens and perhaps hundreds of times could have developed, let's say, a particular expertise in the ways of identifying particles. Is that a fair proposition?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The identification or examination of the shape always presupposes experience. You must always know how different types of gunpowder burn. If we're speaking about partly burned power particles it is clear enough that you need some experience because various types of gunpowder burn differently. So if you're experienced, you will, in any case be better able to determine whether you are looking at an indication for the presence of a certain propellant particle.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you have no reason to believe that the expert -- Macedonian experts which carried out these tests were lacking in that sort of experience. Is that correct? In other words, that they had that sort of experience.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I do not know the Macedonian experts. But I have no reason to suppose that they, during the examination of that gunshot residue, they did not rely on a sufficient experience. I have no knowledge of that, and I'm not trying to insinuate anything of that type.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps before I continue, Your Honour, we have a number of binders or at least one binder for the Judges and for the expert, but I should underline that our very efficient colleague of the Prosecution has already provided you with almost all the documents which are in the binder, but there are two which I believe are missing so we will distribute the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Doctor, you will be given another binder. Doctor, what I'm about to ask you to look at is the statement of one of the expert, one of the Macedonian expert whose name you have seen on the documents given to you and who carried out some of the test.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be under, and, Dr. Eichner, this is under tab 7 of your binder. And This is Rule 65 ter 2D148. This is the OTP statement of Sylvija Kunovska, 21st and 24th October of 2005. And with the registry's assistance, I would kindly ask to go to the third page of that document. That would be paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Doctor, that is page 3 of the statement, the paragraph at the top. Doctor, I will simply read out to you a number of passages from this statement. The First one which is the -- starts at the fourth line on the top of page 3 and it says the following: "The test with diphenylamine is only used as an indication of the possible presence of gunpowder traces. It can confirm the presence of nitrates on a person's hands. Nitrates are also found in fertilisers and other common materials." Doctor, you would agree that this is consistent with what you've said earlier today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you look at the next sentence, Dr. Kunovska has said the following: "Therefore, a positive reaction can occur if the hands are contaminated by one of the substance that contain nitrates." And, again that's consistent with what you said. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: She goes on to explain the following: "However, the appearance and form of nitrates in gunpowder is different from the appearance and form of nitrates found in other substances, and the experienced forensic expert can tell the difference. For example, between nitrate traces left by gunpowder and nitrate traces left by some other material," and again in view of what you said before, you have no reason to take issue with the assertion of Dr. Kunovska. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I understand this to mean that Ms. Kunovska does not doubt this. But let me read it in full before I answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Doctor, there are other passages in the statement which I would like wish to show you at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, first, about this statement. Yes, I'm actually quoting this document. It is the sentence that starts with: "I think that the courts in Macedonia treat the tests, et cetera, [In English] with diphenylamine only as an indication of the presence of gunpowder traces on a person's hand, not as definite proof of the presence of gunpowder." [Interpretation] I can support this statement. This is a correct statement of -- what is described here is an indication indeed, although not a very strong indication. Then Ms. Kunovska continues to -- continues with the statement about the form and shape of the particles. I would say that due to the fact that many plastic materials can burn in the same manner, this can also be an indication that you're looking at gunshot residue. However, with such tests, you cannot arrive at certainty. But each consecutive test will raise the level of certainty. But you will always remain in the area of indications.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you would agree that at least Ms. Kunovska considered that her visual abilities would allow her to raise the level of certainty as to the nature of the particles she was asked to look at. Is that correct? On the basis of the statement that have you in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Visual observation certainly can raise the level of certainty. Every examination that does not result in contradictions to what has been established before will contribute to the significance. Now, the question is how high that significance is. Not very high. But there is a certain possibility that you're indeed looking at gunpowder residue.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you have no reason to challenge the statement of Ms. Kunovska that she felt able to tell gunpowder residue from their appearance from other sort of nitrates. You have no reason to challenge her view on that point?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I would not claim that so strongly. Ms. Kunovska may hold that view. Based on the fact that -- that there is an abundance of nitrate-containing particles that can burn the same way as gunpowder residue, I would be more careful. I think that Ms. Kunovska is offering an indication here that by visual observation you will certainly not decrease your certainty, and her statement that she would be able to distinguish between these two types, but she does not say what significance she would attribute to conclusions based on that, but the diphenylamine test and the visual test certainly can provide indications for the presence of propellant particles but not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You would agree also perhaps with me, a person like Ms. Kunovska who might have applied the test of the paraffin glove test followed by visual inspection perhaps dozens or even hundreds of time might have developed a particular expertise or particular ability in that regard. You would agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt that Ms. Kunovska has great experience in judging how gunpowder residue particles burn. Everybody who works in this field has collected great experience during their years, so I'm sure that is the case with her too. I have no reason to doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And from the documents that you were given by the Prosecution and that you reviewed for the purpose of preparing your report, you have had an opportunity to see that the experts in Macedonia had taken the view that the shape of the particles in any case were consistent at least with gunpowder residue. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is how I interpret this text. I don't doubt that they have carry out these tests with all due carry and that they have adequate experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, for that. And you have also indicated that there would be other factors or other criteria, let's say, that would allow you to perhaps eliminate possible explanations for the source or nature or the particle in question and there's one which I think you have mentioned would be the position of the particle on the hand or the body part that has been tested, is that correct, that the position of the particle, in other words, could be a factor of some relevance to determining the possible nature of the particle?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
