utterances.text: I must correct something you said. You said one particle. One single particle, in my view, tells you nothing about the way it came to the hand where it was found. In rare cases, there are -- there is gunshot residue released backward, which allows you to draw the conclusion that the hand on which that residue was found was indeed the hand that fired a weapon. These traces that we call non-diffuse gunshot residue are very rare, and they occur not even in one case of a thousand. So this gunshot residue is analysed and you find mostly hundreds of particles, and they have a certain shape and position. I have presented an example in my report, and this can even result in hard evidence that we are indeed looking at a hand that fired a weapon. In other cases, based on my experience can you only have indications. That is in cases with diffuse gunshot residue distribution, and that cannot used as hard evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, taking on board your point about the situation where only one particle would be found on the hand, would it be a fair proposition to say that in all 15 cases, in all 15 examples of hands or hand shapes which you were shown by the Prosecution, in all cases, the position of the particle would be either consistent with the use of a gun or, in any case, not inconsistent with such use. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: In the case of the single particles found and that I examined, this is possible. And this is not as inconsistent with the assumption that the hand in question fired a -- a weapon. But you cannot determine with any degree of certainty how that residue arrived on that hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will come to that, Doctor, in a minute. But the point you just made or the answer you just gave would also apply to the other -- the rest of the 15 tests which were given to you. In other words, none of the patterns, if you want to call them that, were inconsistent with someone having shot a gun. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The distributions as depicted on the 15 sketches submitted are consistent with the assumption that these hands may have fired weapons. Supposing, of course tacitly supposing that those particles indeed originate from gunshots.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... And you have also indicated, Doctor -- I'm grateful for your answer. You have also indicated that another factor which could be of some relevance - and I will come back to this in a minute - would be of some assistance, in any case, would the number of particles which would be identified on a particular hand. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I established the number of particles. The maximum was three. The number of particles actually isn't a criterion from which you could draw conclusions. It is more the type of distribution that will let you -- allow to you limit the causes of the application of the particles. But when you have so few particles, a certain form cannot be construed. We are talking about discrete particle distribution without form, and the problem here is that given such a distribution with that form, you cannot limit the possible or delimit the possible causes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So a rule of thumb, for what it's worth scientifically, would be that the more particle, the easier in principle it would be for the expert to determine the exact nature of the particle. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That would certainly be conducive to that goal. If you have a great number of particles, you can distinguish between diffuse and non-diffuse distributions, but if you have a small number of particles, a discrete distribution with great distance between the individual particles, I must say that an identification is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in practice it would be possible to shoot with a gun without any particles appearing on the hand of the shooter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: In very rare cases that is possible. It always depends on the threshold of a certain method. On every weapon, as a rule, you can find certain residue particles, because residue is like dust. Dust is everywhere you look. And the same applies to gunpowder residue on weapons that have been fired at some time or another. It always depends on the sensitivity of the method applied. And on one hand, the weapon may have been cleaned well, then the method may not be all that sensitive or possibly -- for other causes the result of an examination may be negative. There, you -- I must admit you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So that would depend -- I mean, you've indicated, let's say, the scientific side of things but looking at it from the other side, you would agree that the presence or absence of particle or the number thereof would also depend on the type of weapon that is being used and ammunition. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Tendencies are discernible here, namely in various weapons systems, the release of -- of gunshot residue can be greater or smaller. In pistols, for example, if we compare those to other weapons where the chamber does not open automatically after firing a cartridge, there, the quantity of -- of gunshot residue released would be much smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You're giving a hard time to the interpreters. Is that correct, sir, after a certain period of time the particle that would have contaminated a particular part of body would naturally fall off. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is correct. Particles released by firing a cartridge or in any other way connected to shooting or are applied to hands with a good probability will fall off. Even the relevant times have been investigated into. After a few hours, even without washing your hands, the particles will fall off due to any other activity that do you with your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And one of the factor relevant to the length of time that it would take for the particle to fall would be the velocity with which the particle came to the hand. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I do not think there's a link there. The time-frame we are discussing is the time after firing a shot. Let us suppose that a person fires a weapon. On that person's hand, after a few hours, let's say six hours, you would only find few particles, and after ten hours, it is well known that you could not -- you could no longer find particles on that person's hands, at least not using the current methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: There would be all sorts of intervening factors which could play a role in the quicker elimination of the particles such as let's say the rain or the person washing his or her hands. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Anything which disturbs these particles which are not stuck -- stuck hard on to the surface, anything could influence them. So this is a latent indication that things will change.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is it possible also, Doctor, that the relatively limited number of particles which were mentioned on the drawings which you were shown is the result of the particular working methods used by your colleagues from Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I think that the use of wax has transferred the particles from the skin with success and I think that the folio that we use or alcohol or other tests that we use -- well, I think that the particles, the transfer of the particles with wax is successful in removing most of the particles from the surface of the skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: What about the later part of the process, sir, is that possible that the local expert would exclude from their analysis or, rather from their conclusions a number of particles which were indeed detached by the chemical reaction but which they could not positively identify as gunpowder? Could that be the reason for the limited numbers of particles on the drawings?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: It could be a reason, it could be. But it could also be a reason that particles were hidden by the wax, but we can't know that. Normally wax and other materials which have been solidified are satisfactory for removing particles. Ninety percent of them can be -- of gunpowder residue can be removed from pores by this method, so the detection of the particles is usually okay. Whether this was perfect in this case, I don't know, with the diphenylamine process.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, perhaps to help us decide which one of the two explanation are the perhaps more likely in this case, I'd like you again, Doctor, if you could, to look at the same statement of Ms. Kunovska. And it is it on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: For the registry's benefit, it's still Rule 65 ter 2D148 at page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, Doctor, I'll ask to you look at paragraph 7 of that statement where Ms. Kunovska was asked to look at particular results of Mr. Farush Mehmedi, which is, I understand, one of the results that was also given to you.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Could I have a moment here so that I can read the passage in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Doctor, I will read for the transcript the relevant page of this paragraph. It starts with the word however. Five line from the bottom of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DR. KUNOVSKA SAYS THIS
utterances.text: "However, if the expert performing the analysis does not think that the nitrate particle came from gunpowder, most probably he or she will not mark the particle on the sketch of the hand or mention it in the result. That depends on the forensic expert. My report from 17 August describe the positive reaction for nitrate." So again, Doctor, if one relies upon the statement of Ms. Kunovska for that purpose, you would agree that perhaps one of the factor which played a role in the limited number of particle on the sketch is the fact that some experts in Macedonia would only identify on the sketch those particles which they have positively identified as gunpowder. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful, and that was a fair enough answer. Doctor, you would agree that, in practice, the test as applied by the Macedonian experts came in two phases. The first one which you have already explained was to review for each and every paraffin glove test the nature of the material in question, and at a later stage the experts were asked to draw certain conclusion on the basis of the entirety of the record as to what this could be. Is that agreeable to you?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I understood from the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And there's a particular document, Doctor, which I would like to show you which is one of the documents that was given to you by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, and, Doctor, under tab 8 of your binder. This is Rule 65 ter 69 and it has an ERN N000-0021. The Macedonian version would be N000-0017.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recall being given a copy of that document by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I don't remember such a document. At least not -- oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I do remember such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful. As can you see from this document, it registered the names of the 33rd persons or villagers who were subjected to the paraffin glove test. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I remember this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that correct, Doctor, that the 33 names which appear on the first page of that document are the names of the people who were subjected to the paraffin glove test by the Macedonian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I would have to check all the information to tell you, but I would assume you are right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: But I would need to check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Doctor, for your confidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Simply for Your Honour's assistance, the names which are underlined in the list are those which have been tested positive to the paraffin glove test, as is apparent from the following paragraph and the next page. I'd kindly ask the registry to turn to the second page of that document, please. That would be further down the page in the Macedonian version -- no, that's -- that would be N000-0022, please. Thank you. And in the Macedonian version, that will still be the same document, the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If I can draw your attention, Doctor, to the sentence which follow the list of names. Can you see that in the paper copy or the electronic copy which starts with the word: "The location of the found." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And he says -- it says: "The location of the found gunshot residues is given in the pattern attached," and there follows a number. Do you recall registering your disapproval of this finding?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Just a moment, I have to read this again. I don't remember that I did not agree with these three paragraphs. What is said here is simply that gunshot residue was found and that on the enclosed pictures they were noted, the residues were sketched on to the pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in your --

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: And nothing else is said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in your report, Doctor, you pointed out that in fact the mere subjection to the paraffin glove test would reveal not the presence of gunshot residue per se but the presence of nitrite particles. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The reaction with diphenylamine is -- or shows the presence of nitrates. But a reaction could occur with other non-nitrate substances.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if these documents had mention that on the location was found nitrate particles instead of gunshot residues, you would have agreed with the sentence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: If the wording had been "indications of nitrate deposits," then I would agree. But it would have been helpful to say what substances aside from nitrate could result, could cause a reaction here.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Doctor, I don't mean to torture you with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is simply to bring to the attention of the Chamber that the English translation is inaccurate and that the Macedonian version refers to nitrate particles as the doctor agreed with in a way in this sentence I have read to the doctor as well as in the following sentence, and that the translation as gunshot residues in those two sentence is inaccurate and that point was also made by Dr. Kunovska in her own interview with the Office of the Prosecutor at paragraph 3. And among the disclosure there is also a memorandum by the Prosecution highlighting the fact that this translation is in fact wrong and could be in fact be misleading, so we would simply suggest that the translation -- or that CLSS be asked to re-translate this document to reflect the accurate content of the Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Doctor, I have a question perhaps which is more in the field of statistics than pure forensic science. But would you be able to say in a random population how many people would test positive to nitrate particles, if the paraffin glove test with diphenylamine chemical reaction? Are you aware of any studies or any discussion of that matter?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: This would be have to be tested, but I do not know if any such tests having been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Are you aware of any approximate figure in that regard, or is it simply a matter that you don't know about?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I do not know of any such tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And we've already discussed earlier, is it correct that after the Macedonian experts had given their views about each and every one of the particular tests, they were then asked by the Court to provide an overall assessment as to what they believed to be the particles in question, what they believed those particles were made of?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Could I read your question once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, the question was too long and not particularly clear. I will phrase it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps after the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you think that will help restore you, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's poor Dr. Eichner who will need the break, I suspect. We will have the second break now and resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like to turn your mind to the second part of the -- let's say the -- the second phase of the process followed by the Macedonian authority and that's the time when having rendered their initial report that there had been 16 positive reaction to nitrate particles, they were then asked by the Court to state their view as to whether these particles could or couldn't be considered as gunpowder residue. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I'm not sure now which report you're referring to. You mean the -- the report where the Macedonian experts --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I have lost the translation, but I was talking in general terms, sir, about the process or the procedure which had been followed by the Macedonian authorities in this matter. I wasn't specifically relating to your report. Do you recall that that's the course, in fact, that the Macedonian authorities followed?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that a correct understanding that to do so, the Macedonian expert looked at, if you want, the ensemble or the group of reports which they had prepared and considered the matter as a whole to give their opinion to the Court? Is that the way you understand it as well?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I suppose that you mean this report here in front of me from your binder. Is this the report you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, I will direct you to one of those report, if you wish. That would be report under tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is part of Exhibit P47 and it has an ERN of ET-0463-8982-01 and the Macedonian equivalent would be 0463-8891-092.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Doctor, this is again one of the documents which was given to you by the Prosecution to prepare your report.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I remember this phrasing. I cannot see the number I received, but I remember the phrasing from the other reports I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And indeed there were two similar reports or two reports that look similar. But the question is, Doctor, is that correct what the authorities did in this case is to consider, if you want, to consolidate a group of individual reports which they had made in relation to particular individual and to give their opinion as to whether, as a group, those could be considered to be consistent or whether or not those could be regarded -- those particles, that is, could be regarded as gunpowder residue?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: These reports state that, as they put it in the last paragraph and this also is the gist of all other reports -- let me now quote in English: [In English] "Based on their shape" - it's here in English - "form, location and dispersion, it can be confirmed with a large possibility that the above-mentioned particles have gunpowder." [Interpretation] This is a different phrasing with a similar meaning as in the reports that I was provided. So it isn't a verbatim match but the meaning is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct, Doctor. We believe that one of the documents refer to a large possibility whereas the one refers to a large probability and it may indeed be only a translation mistake. Is that correct, however, that this finding or this conclusion which is drawn by the expert in this particular report refers to the result as pertained to the eight individuals which are mentioned in the first paragraph of that report?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I would check that -- I would have to check that in detail, whether these are indeed the persons mentioned in the report that were provided to me. But I suppose that you already checked that, because I would have to check it now and I couldn't answer a question as I stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, the question, Doctor, is more of a scientific technique or scientific method I'm interested in. Is that correct that it is an acceptable scientific method in general to evaluate let's say a number of items together as a whole which you have studied, as you did, for instance, in your own report about three guns. Let me perhaps explain that further. If you have identified different object, it would be scientifically acceptable to then consider them as an ensemble, as a group, to see whether the probabilities of a particular result are higher rather than lower. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This approach is always legitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And what appears to be the case from this report is that, in fact, the course that was followed by the Macedonian expert considered the results of those eight individuals as a whole, is that correct, on the face of this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That may depend on the circumstances, how and what relations those persons were among themselves. If you select at random eight persons from a larger group at different places and try to group them together, then you will have fewer results than -- than when you have eight neighbouring persons with the same pattern of movement and behaviour in the past. In that case, such an approach would make sense, or could make sense, and would be more significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And would it be correct or a correct way to understand this document, to see that the experts who were asked for their opinions took those factors into consideration and using their own professional and scientific expertise or experience came to the conclusion which you have read out in the last paragraph. Is that what seems to have happened in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Which paragraph are you referring to, the last one? But where do you see the approach that these findings were grouped? I haven't found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't my original question, Doctor, and if you look at the first paragraph of this document you will see that there is a list of names that are mentioned and those are a part or a group of the people, of the 16 people which were mentioned in the previous document that were shown to him. And as appears to be the case in this document, this -- the foils that were the result of the particle test were considered by this expert, Mr. Uslinkovski and another expert as a group. Do you have any reason to believe that it's not the case, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: No. I just -- I'm not yet familiar with this document, so please allow me to search for this alleged conclusion by Ms. Kunovska, because I haven't been able to find it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, there is a very similar document, if you can turn to the next page of your binder, that may assist you. This is a similar document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is part of exhibit P50 and it has an ERN ET-9002-0184-1. And the Macedonian would be N002-0084-101.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If you look at the bottom left, Doctor, you will find the signature or, in any case, the name of Ms. Kunovska.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that correct that on the face of this document it would appear that in fact the report, this particular report as opposed to the individual report prepared together considered, if you want, the results of the nitrite particle test, the diphenylamine test, as a group in relation to the eight particular individuals which are mentioned in this document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I do not yet know such a document. But perhaps you can help me by indicating the precise spot where Ms. Kunovska is -- is making such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, if the witness can be shown, once again, the document which is Rule 65 ter 2D148. That is under tab 7, Dr. Eichner. This is in your binder, tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if the registry could go to page number 3 of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it now. And maybe you can now show me the spot where Ms. Kunovska summarizes in this fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will read the last two sentences of this paragraph for you. It says: "We concluded that on the basis of the form, distribution and location of these nitrite particles, it can be confirmed with great probability that these nitrite particles originated from gunpowder. We base our scientific opinion on the result of forensic analysis such as that provided for Mehmedi Farush described above in our professional experience."

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So would you agree with the proposition, sir, with what appears to have happened in this particulars case is that indeed Ms. Kunovska and her colleagues, once they had given individual views about individual results, were then asked and gave their opinion as to two particular groups of tests considered as a whole, is that correct, does that appear to be consistent with the evidence or the information of Ms. Kunovska?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I think that this approach is something that can be considered, but I cannot find it anywhere. Maybe you can point out that sentence to me where Ms. Kunovska summarizes the results for several persons. I do not know this document yet, but you certainly know it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, sir, we would have to go answer to tab 15, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And for the registry's benefit, this would be Exhibit P50 with an ERN ET-N002-0184-1. And the Macedonian version would be N002-0084-101.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, Doctor, the conclusion which I think you are seeking and which you reprinted in your report is the last paragraph in that particular document starting with the word: "Based on their form." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This sentence is -- can be considered a conclusion from the reports that were provided to me. I -- but I interpret it as applying to one particular person, but because the text that I read so far does not allow for other conclusions, I think that, however, that it may be justified to form groups in order to check the significance or validity of a certain result. As I said, this is a legitimate approach, but I cannot find this approach in Ms. Kunovska's text. I understand this to mean that she's referring to individual results pertaining to individual persons. She never mentions, Ms. Kunovska never mentions summaries, so that's why I don't understand the basis for this interpretation of yours. I repeat, that I consider this approach to be legitimate, but I cannot find it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you would agree that based on the statement of Ms. Kunovska and the fact that she use the plural in the last sentence of that paragraph where she referred to the results, as opposed to the result, it's at least upon to interpret the document which is now in front of you and the finding which is in the last paragraph as a finding which pertains to a group of individuals and a group of findings rather than to individual findings. Do you agree that it's a reading that is open?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I suppose that can't be ruled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And just before I turn to a number of other matters, sir, and to wrap this in a sort of a summary form, would it be correct that what appears to be the case from this document and from other parts of what was read to you earlier, there's a number of indication, if you wish, that have been taken into account by the authorities to come to the conclusion that they have, that this was probably gunpowder residue. And I'm going to put each and every one of them to you and you will tell me whether you agree or not that this was indeed a factor of relevance. The first factor which the authorities appear to have taken into account to come to that conclusion was the fact that indeed there was a positive result to diphenylamine which is an indication of the presence of nitrate. Is that one of the factor which they appear to have taken into account?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: This conclusion was drawn from the reports, at least based on the text that was provided to me. But Ms. Kunovska herself did not confirm that, did not corroborate that. In her letter, under 7, she says that she does not refer to gunshot residue but to nitrate particles.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And my question was precisely this, sir: Although the presence of nitrate particle would in no case be sufficient to conclude that this indeed is it gunpowder, that would at least be one factor pointing in that direction. Is that correct? Point in that possible direction, in any case.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Certainly. The presence of nitrate is an indication of a small value, but it is an indication for gunshot residue, just like other nitrate particles, and other particles that test positively with diphenylamine. But, yeah, it is an indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And another indication which the authorities appear to have taken into consideration is the form of the particle in question, and again you will agree that this is an indication or a possible indication that the particle in question was indeed gunpowder. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is correct. It is an indication. However, you would have to see that in the context of particles that burn similarly, such as TNT. When TNT burns you get very similar structures and particles, particles of a very similar shape, and it is extremely difficult to keep them apart. Those are not particles that are gunshot residue.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We're going to come to the TNT in a moment, Doctor. I'd just like to go through these factors at first. Another factor which the authorities mention as being relevant to their assessment is the location on which the particle was found, and again I think you have agreed that the location might indeed assist the expert in determining whether the particle in question could be gunpowder or not, although you have indicated that in some cases the value of this could be quite limited. But, as a matter of principle it could be relevant. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The presence of nitrate containing particles is always an indication. But a mere indication; no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And another indication which you've mention is the positioning or dispersion, to use a more technical term, of the particles in question. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And another consideration which would be legitimate from a scientific point of view would be to take into consideration the consistency or similarities between various results of individual tests. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: It is certainly permissible to act in accordance with such an approach and to draw conclusions from that. Yes. That is a legitimate approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And would the high percentage of positive result be also of assistance to an expert who would wish to make determination or draw conclusions about the nature of the contamination?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid not much. There's always a certain amount of uncertainty when you're faced with indications alone, because you could draw the conclusion that all persons had the same substance on their hands, but without a more detailed test, you cannot prove that, and you must also allow for different conclusions, such as that those were actually nitrate particles of a different type.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will come to your empirical hypothesis which I have called. I think you have found a better term. But would it be correct to say or to conclude that all of the factors which I have mention to you and which appear to have been taken into consideration by the Macedonian authority were all consistent with their findings or at least were not inconsistent with the finding they've made. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: One could say that the results of the Macedonian police are consistent with all the hypotheses in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But would it be correct, Doctor, that all the factors, the presence of nitrate, the shape, and all of the other factors which I have mentioned to you, all of them were either consistent with the finding made or, in any case, not inconsistent with the finding made by the Macedonian authority. Is that a correct conclusion?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The results as to the presence of nitrate particles can be evaluated as the presence of gunpowder particles, and then there was this next level of interpretation, another level, but insofar, this interpretation is permissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the next level which you are indicated was in effect exercised by the expert in their own scientific and professional expertise and based on the criteria which I have listed, they drew the conclusion that in their view, in any case, there was a high probability of the material in question being gunpowder residue. Is that what appears to have happened?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: This conclusion can be seen in the text. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that also correct that none of the factor which we have listed, whether it be the positive result, whether it be the shape or the structure or the position of the particle, none of those would have militated against the finding made by the Macedonian authority. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: You mean against the finding that it was gunpowder residue?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I will rephrase it in a better way, which you've used earlier. Is that correct that each factor, whether individually or in combination, increased the probability of the accuracy of the finding made by the Macedonian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: You are referring to the two levels of the use of diphenylamine and the microscopic analysis, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Here one could say that the use of diphenylamine with a positive reaction would be a certain indication - not much but a certain indication - for the presence of nitrate particles, or gunpowder residue, the microscopic analysis would be a further indication that the first -- that would support the first result. To what extent is supports the first result is an open question. But you are right. These two steps are certainly -- certainly reinforce one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that is true of the other elements as well. If -- if the evidence given by Ms. Kunovska or the information given by Ms. Kunovska to the Prosecution, namely that she was able to identify gunpowder particles from the shape thereof, this fact would also militate in favour of the finding which is drawn by the Macedonian authority. You would agree?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it is acceptable to draw a conclusion from the form to -- with certainty or to a large extent that they are gunpowder residue. This is my criticism, because if you see how TNT, the explosive TNT burns, and it is very similar to gunpowder residue, and when it burns, you won't see much difference to other particles, and I'm speaking about visual observation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you agree, Doctor -- you have no reason to believe that Ms. Kunovska would not have been able to do that and on the face of her statement she would seem to be able to make that discrimination between gunpowder particle on the one hand and other particles; is that correct? That's what her statement suggests.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That's the way one could understand it. But in her text, I see that she talks simply about indications, and I assume that Ms. Kunovska is aware that the appearance is not sufficient for full interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I will read perhaps to you once again the relevant paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUNOVSKA SAYS THIS
utterances.text: "The appearance and form of nitrates in gunpowder is different from the appearance and form of nitrates found in other substance." And you would agree, Doctor, that -- and that's paragraph 6, top of page 3, if you want to look at it, under tab 7, you would agree that she doesn't seem to qualify in any way her ability to tell gunpowder residue from any other sort of nitrate particles? It's tab 7, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I would be interested here in knowing from her, from Ms. Kunovska, how gunpowder residue can be distinguished from partially burned TNT visually. If she could do that, then I would be very interested in learning what she has to say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I would like to turn now to a number of hypotheses. I'm sorry if the term is not adequate. I would adopt the one which you propose. I think you've talked about empirical scenarios or empirical proposal. And you've raised a number of hypotheticals, call them that, which could possibly explain the presence of nitrate particles or even gunpowder particles on the hands of the people who were tested, and in your report you list a number of those, and I'd like to go with you through each of those. The first one or the first indication which you give of the first scenario which you consider is the one which would concern the carrying or the handling of a gun by a person who is being tested for nitrate particle and what you state in your report is that the mere handling of a gun or the carrying of a gun or the change of a magazine in a gun could in itself be sufficient to result in nitrate particle being -- contaminating a hand and therefore in a positive result in the paraffin test. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And simply to clarify this matter with you, Doctor, you would agree that the Macedonian expert, when they have drawn their conclusion, have not said otherwise. In other words, they haven't suggested that the persons who had tested positive had shot from a gun as opposed to merely handled or carried a gun. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is correct. Ms. Kunovska speaks of the presence of gunpowder residue and of an indication that the particles were found on the hands. Thus, there is an indication of the possibility of a shot being made by the hand in question. This is correct. However, there's something missing here in what she says: The fact that there are other possibilities which would bring about this situation. But as to the shooting of a weapon, as she says, as an indication, it is quite possible and quite true.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, perhaps it's an issue of translation. I would ask to you again to go to tab 15, please, of your binder. That would be exhibit P50. It has an ERN ET N002-0184-1, in the English. And N002-0084-101 for the Macedonian version. Again, Doctor, this is the same document with the signature of Ms. Kunovska at the ... And if I may draw your attention again on the last paragraph which contains their ultimate conclusion on the question that was asked of them. Dr. Kunovska and Mr. Uslinkovski say that their conclusion is that "Based on their form, location and position, it can be determined with a great probability that these nitrate particles originate from gunpowder." My question is this. Perhaps it's a misunderstanding as to the answer given, but would you agree that at least as far as the ultimate conclusion is concerned, they do not seem to have taken a view that it was either from a shot or from the handling of a gun that this gunpowder had come on to the hands of the people?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Motoike.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOTOIKE
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. But -- sorry, Dr. Eichner. But perhaps there is some confusion in the way that the question was actually translated or the way it was stated, with respect to "ultimate conclusion," because I believe that Dr. Eichner was referring in his prior answer to one of the paragraphs which I think is located in the third paragraph of this particular document, so there may be a confusion accusation as to what the doctor considers to be the ultimate conclusion as opposed to what counsel refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. I will try to clarify that, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Doctor, could you explain perhaps for the assistance of the Court if and whether you understood Ms. Kunovska indeed to have made a finding that the results were the result of having firing a weapon or whether you understood that she did not make such a finding, and if she has or if you understood her to have done so, on what particular part of the document you understood that she made such a finding.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I can read her text in the following manner. Or I interpret it in the following way. She sees a possibility that shoot -- firing a weapon could be a possibility for these particles. This is in the second-last paragraph. In the last paragraph, she gives her view of the situation that the nitrate particles found in her analysis could -- can be determined with a great possibility to be from gunpowder. This is what she says.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, could it be read in another way. And I'm going to show you another document to assist you in that respect. Could it be that in fact the finding of Ms. Kunovska, the ultimate finding, to call it that, was that the result or the finding which they made was the result -- the finding which was made was simply that the matter appeared to them to be of gunpowder nature and not necessarily that it had resulted from the use of a weapon. And I will draw your attention again to the statement of Ms. Kunovska which is under your tab 7, Doctor, and with an ERN Rule 65 ter 2D148 and it is again at page 3. And again, Doctor, I understand that did you not have the benefit of Ms. Kunovska's statement at the time when you prepared your report, so it's not a criticism of you. But I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 8 of that statement, more particularly on the last sentence but one of that paragraph, where Ms. Kunovska concludes this -- state this: "We concluded that on the basis of the form, distribution and location of these nitrate particles it can be confirmed with great probability that this nitrate particles originated with -- from gunpowder." Can you see that, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So if that had been indeed or if it is indeed the ultimate conclusion which was reached by the authorities, the Macedonian authorities, you would agree that they would have at least considered some of the hypotheses which you put forward; namely that the contamination could have resulted not only from the shooting of a gun, but from the carrying or the handling of a gun or magazine loaded with ammunition. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: This hypothesis of yours is possible, but I don't see how that derives from Ms. Kunovska's texts here. So I can't really say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: As I mentioned, Doctor, I understand that you didn't have the benefit of Ms. Kunovska's statement, and you agree that to the extent that the document which you had was ambiguous, it is in any case possible to read the finding of Ms. Kunovska to have been limited to the presence of gunpowder as opposed to a finding that this was due to the shooting of a gun.

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: I see in her writings that the stress is on residue, on residue from a weapon. To what extent the person in question used a weapon, shot a weapon, I would think are secondary here, in her words. She refers to the possibility and -- but does not refer to other possibilities, but primarily what she says is that there is a presence of nitrate particles, which she interprets as gunpowder residue. That is the essence of her report.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I would like to turn to a second of the scenarios or the hypotheses which is drawn in your report, and you've indicated that another manner in which contamination with nitrate particle could occur or with -- specifically with gunpowder in this case would be a situation where someone would be shot at relatively close range and deposit would attach to the T-shirt or the clothing of that person and another person would then touch the clothing in question. Is that correct? That's another way in which contamination could occur?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: Yes, this is another possibility for contamination.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that is correct, Doctor, that in order for the T-shirt to be contaminated in the first place, this would mean that the shot was a close-range shot within or under less than two metres distance. Is that correct, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The probability of -- of contamination un -- under two metres is possible but not more. And I would assume that the test -- that the diphenylamine test is not sufficient to detect such microscopic particles being transported through the air, because they're very small, and I don't think that one could come to such a conclusion here. But one cannot exclude the possibility of air transport of the particles.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps to follow on your last comment. Did you have information in the material that was provided to you by the Prosecution that this particular type of transfer of particles could have occurred in this particular case in any of the 15 case that you have reviewed? Do you have any information or did you have any evidence that this could have happened in any of those cases?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You've also indicated that another manner in which transfer of nitrate particles could occur would be in a situation where an individual would touch with his hand, for instance, an object that is itself contaminated with nitrate particle or gunpowder, is that correct, is that a mechanism of transfer?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: This is another possible mechanism of transfer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct that the particle in question would attach to that part of body with which the person would touch the contaminated object. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: That is correct. The first contact would mean that the particles were on the place of original contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if for instance an individual were to grab with his hand let's say the piece of a shell or a piece of shrapnel, the residue, if you wish, would attach to that part of the hand which has touched the shell or the shrapnel in question. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: The greatest density would be here, one would expect it here, of contact, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that would mean in the example given of someone touching a piece of shrapnel with his hand, you would expect to find the residue on the inside of the house -- on the inside of the hand. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMON EICHNER
utterances.text: We don't know how a person might have had contact with shrapnel from a grenade. It could be with the hand, it could be another type of contact. But you are right, where the first contact is, with the skin, is where the greatest density of particles will be. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps for the benefit of everyone, I'm about to launch into a relatively lengthy, in any case a ten-minute part of the cross-examination and I was wondering whether the Court would be willing to break at this stage or whether you would like me to continue and use the three or four minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We accept your indication and will adjourn for the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps before we do, Your Honour, a simple matter that I have omitted to do at an earlier stage. I have shown to the witness what was Rule 65 ter, that's the Prosecution list 69, which is under tab 8 of the Defence binder, we would simply wish the document to be marked for identification at this stage, until that time when we receive the CLSS translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As exhibit 1D146, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps to assist the Chamber, we would definitely hope to be finish well within the next -- the first session of tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mettraux. I'm sure Dr. Eichner will be pleased to hear that. We adjourn now. We resume again tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of September, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
